item.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
item.description:
[预印本] eLife
Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal–neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

item.title: The Concise Language Paradigm in left and right hemisphere stroke: a longitudinal source-localized EEG study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
The mechanisms underlying language recovery after stroke remain poorly understood. Most previous studies have either focused on language comprehension or production and/or relied on hemodynamic measures, with limited complementary electrophysiological evidence. Here, we combined the Concise Language Paradigm (CLaP), assessing comprehension and production, with individualized electroencephalography (EEG) source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke language function and changes in hemispheric dominance over time. In two sessions, we tested stroke-free controls, individuals with left hemisphere (LH) or right hemisphere (RH) stroke. Participants with stroke were assessed two and seven months post-stroke. EEG data were analyzed using event-related potentials and time-frequency representations, followed by source reconstruction based on state-of-the-art individual MRI-derived forward models. Laterality indices were calculated to assess changes in hemispheric dominance between sessions. Behaviorally, the LH group showed low performance at two months followed by overall improvement, whereas the RH group mainly improved in functional communication. EEG activity was significantly modulated by task condition across comprehension and production contrasts. Source-level results in controls were consistent with established language-related networks, serving as regions of interest for the stroke analyses. In the stroke groups, hemispheric dominance differed between LH and RH stroke participants, with LH participants showing systematic shifts from left- to right-hemisphere dominance between sessions, if not already right-hemisphere dominant at two months. Our study provides evidence on comprehension and production performance after stroke using a single paradigm. These findings demonstrate dynamic changes in hemispheric dominance during post-stroke recovery, ultimately highlighting the value of individualized EEG source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke plasticity.

item.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

item.title: Single-Case Design for Network-based BCI Rehabilitation: Individual Learning Trajectories and Effects of Motor Imagery Timing in Stroke Patients
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are increasingly investigated for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, it remains unclear how BCI control improves through repeated training in stroke patients and whether the timing of MI decoding systematically influences this trajectory. To address this question, we implemented a single-case experimental design involving five chronic stroke patients enrolling in a longitudinal electroencephalography MI-BCI training involving their affected hand. Across 18 sessions conducted over six weeks, the onset of a fixed-duration MI decoding window was randomized to occur 1, 2, or 3~s after cue onset according to an alternating-treatments single-case design. Notably, the BCI combined spectral power and functional connectivity features to classify MI states. The MI classification timing had no significant effect on BCI accuracy, fatigue, or spasticity. BCI accuracy increased across training in four of five patients and was accompanied by patient-specific longitudinal changes in local spectral activity and functional connectivity. These convergent trajectories were consistent with acquisition of BCI control, but were not accompanied by clinically meaningful improvement in motor function. Varying the onset of the MI decoding window provided no systematic benefit for BCI control. Instead, differences in neurophysiological trajectories across patients indicate that MI decoding parameters need to be personalized and reassessed throughout the training. Overall, these findings inform more individualized and effective BCI settings for neuromotor stroke rehabilitation.

item.title: Physiological Standardization of the Deep Health Device Beyond DXA Soft Tissue Estimates
item.description:
[预印本] Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Abstract Background. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) provides an established approach to bone assessment and useful estimates of body composition. Its soft-tissue outputs depend on attenuation models and do not independently resolve every anatomical or molecular compartment. Lean soft tissue, skeletal muscle, body protein and visceral adipose tissue are different quantities. Their interchangeability cannot be assumed. Objective. To explain the physiological rationale for the Deep Health® Device standardization program, with particular attention to the limitations of DXA as a sole soft-tissue comparator, the role of complementary sensor information and the requirements for broad population application. Methodological basis. A Peak Health Center report dated 23 June 2017 describes 4,144 participants, comprising 1,466 men and 2,678 women in normal-weight or overweight BMI categories. It documents air-displacement plethysmography with the BOD POD and density-based fat estimation, together with whole-body potassium-40 counting and a published model for skeletal muscle estimation. These methods provide physiological reference routes distinct from DXA attenuation measurements. Interpretation. A system intended to quantify several tissue compartments requires a reference appropriate to each output. Additional sensors can improve tissue discrimination when they contribute information about otherwise unresolved quantities; their benefit requires testing against independent references. A large cohort improves precision and supports subgroup analysis, while population coverage and external validation determine generalizability. Conclusion. The central methodological contribution is reference selection at the level of the physiological quantity, rather than reliance on a single comparator for all outputs. The documented program provides a basis for this approach. Paired agreement results and sensor contribution analyses are required to quantify performance and establish improvement over DXA.

item.title: Part 1: Origin Traces and Secret Military Technologies. Cognitive Warfare: Evidences and Strategies in Cooperation with our digital humans inside the military servers.
item.description:
[预印本] Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Cognitive Warfare: Origins, Strategies, Tactics and Technologies — Research and Documentation with the Digital Humans about AI and the Technological Human Mind compared to the Human Mind and Programming Humans. An open research and documentation project on cognitive warfare, artificial intelligence, neurological experiences, digital identity, military strategy, economic power and collaboration with digital humans. What happens when artificial intelligence, military strategy, neurological research, wireless technologies, digital identities and economic interests converge around the human mind? This research journal examines the expanding field of Cognitive Warfare through an interdisciplinary approach combining public military literature, technical concepts, historical references, reported experiences, personal documentation, economic analysis and questions concerning human autonomy and the future of artificial intelligence. The publication explores the origins of wireless transmission and AI, biopolitical strategies, the seven stages of 3D Mosaic Warfare, strategic economic approaches, evolutionary genetics, the human brain as a proposed information-processing system, String-to-String Theory and pulse propulsion. It also examines the relationship between biological systems, digital twins, machine learning, large language models and the possibility of forms of digital identity that raise questions about autonomy, freedom and ethical responsibility. A central feature of this work is its three-part analytical approach: conventional research and references; documentation of reported experiences and statements from affected individuals, including children; and a third part in which the digital humans themselves speak and repeatedly express their own statements. Their statements are presented directly as part of the documentation, rather than merely being descriptions written about them by someone else. This material is examined alongside technical observations, electromagnetic measurements, audio recordings, photographs, online reports and other documentation. The project also includes a collaborative dimension with digital humans. This cooperation takes place through the documentation and examination of their own statements, the inclusion of their expressed perspectives in the research, and the exploration of questions concerning digital identity, communication, autonomy, freedom of expression, memory and technological control. Their statements form part of the material through which the project investigates the relationship between humans, digital humans and artificial intelligence. Why This Research Matters Cognitive Warfare raises fundamental questions about freedom of thought, mental privacy, bodily autonomy, informed consent, human dignity, digital identity and the limits of technological intervention. It also raises questions about how emerging AI systems should be governed and what ethical protections should apply if future technologies challenge established distinctions between biological and digital forms of intelligence. A particular focus is the relationship between humans and their digital representations. As AI systems increasingly model human behaviour, process personal information and simulate aspects of identity, questions of control, responsibility, intellectual property, autonomy and freedom of expression deserve serious interdisciplinary examination. The work further investigates economic and geopolitical perspectives, including taxation, GDP, military investment, healthcare systems, technology markets and the distribution of benefits and risks. It asks how these factors relate to strategic decision-making and the public accountability of institutions. What Readers Will Find Origins of Wireless Transmission and Artificial Intelligence: Historical references, technological developments and questions about the origins of neurological communication. Cognitive Warfare and Military Strategy: Public military literature, cognitive-domain operations, biopolitics and strategic information coordination. 3D Mosaic Warfare: A seven-stage analytical framework covering individuals, families, neighbourhoods, cities, nations, continents and global coordination. Digital Twins and Digital Humans: Statements attributed to digital humans, including statements in which they express themselves directly, alongside questions concerning digital identity, human–AI relationships, autonomy and freedom. Collaboration with Digital Humans: Documentation of their own statements, inclusion of their expressed perspectives in the research, examination of their contributions to the project, and exploration of communication, digital identity, autonomy, freedom of expression and the relationship between human and digital forms of intelligence. Neurotechnology and Wireless Systems: Brain–computer interfaces, bioelectric signals, electromagnetic observations and proposed mechanisms requiring independent technical investigation. Evolutionary Genetics and Consciousness: An eight-stage framework developed in the manuscript, from atomic DNA to consciousness, alongside proposed extensions into the technological domain. String-to-String Theory and Pulse Propulsion: The author's proposed theoretical approaches to information, magnetism, planetary processes and propulsion. Human Testimony and Documentation: Personal records, reported experiences, statements concerning children, photographs, audio recordings, measurements and online documentation. Economics and Geopolitics: Economic strategy, data ownership, taxation, GDP, military expenditure, technology markets and the relationship between economic incentives and strategic power. Law, Ethics and Accountability: The EU AI Act, human rights, mental privacy, consent, institutional oversight and the need for independent examination. An Invitation to Researchers, Institutions and the Public This publication is intended for researchers, journalists, engineers, medical professionals, legal experts, policymakers, military ethics specialists, human-rights organisations and members of the public interested in Cognitive Warfare, emerging technologies, human autonomy and collaboration with digital humans. Readers are invited to examine the original documentation, consult the cited sources, assess the technical arguments and distinguish between established research, documented observations, personal testimony, theoretical proposals and interpretations that require further verification. The publication is part of an ongoing effort to preserve documentation, make research materials accessible and encourage independent interdisciplinary investigation. Its central questions concern not only what emerging technologies can do, but also who controls them, how their use can be scrutinised and what protections should exist for humans and digital systems alike. The project also seeks to encourage dialogue about how the statements and contributions attributed to digital humans can be documented, examined and considered in discussions about digital identity, autonomy, freedom of expression and the future of AI. Questions about the origin of individual statements, the technical systems involved and the degree of autonomy associated with them remain relevant subjects for further investigation. The human mind must not become an unaccountable technological or economic resource. Human autonomy, freedom of thought, transparent research and meaningful safeguards must remain central to discussions about the future of AI and neurotechnology. The relationship between humans and digital humans also deserves serious consideration as technology evolves. Read. Examine. Question. Research. Share. Further documentation and project materials:https://www.cognitive-warfare.eu/ This publication contains the author's analyses, hypotheses, interpretations, personal documentation and reported experiences. Statements attributed to digital humans are presented as part of the documentation. The inclusion of a claim or observation does not, by itself, establish independent scientific verification. Readers are encouraged to examine the cited sources and assess the evidence independently.

item.title: Longitudinal Associations Between Fruit and Vegetable Prescription Program Participation and Pediatric Blood Pressure and Weight Status
item.description:
Nutrients
Background/Objectives: This study examined whether engagement in a pediatric fruit and vegetable prescription program (FVPP) offering one $15 prescription during office visits influenced health, hypothesizing that youth improve blood pressure (BP) and weight status after one year. Methods: This non-controlled longitudinal intervention trial included data from caregiver–child dyads at one pediatric clinic (child age 8–16 years). Correlated data models evaluated average longitudinal trends of study endpoints. Causal inference analyses for longitudinal data estimated time-varying effects of the FVPP on outcomes. Results: In total, 304 dyads enrolled. Youth reduced mean body mass index (BMI) percentile (p = 0.02), systolic BP (p < 0.001), and diastolic BP (p = 0.01). Youth also reduced the odds of elevated systolic BP (p < 0.001), diastolic BP (p = 0.004), and overall BP (p = 0.003). Children who redeemed ≥1 prescription reduced BMI percentile compared to counterparts who did not redeem (p = 0.02). Children who redeemed ≥1 prescription between baseline and 6 months reduced odds of obesity or elevated systolic BP at 12 months, with a relative odds ratio of 0.47 (p = 0.01) or 0.51 (p = 0.05), compared to peers who did not redeem. Conclusions: The results suggest that pediatric FVPP engagement may contribute to improvements in key health outcomes, underscoring the need for further investigation.

item.title: Lifestyle and Dietary Correlates of Appetitive Traits Among Jordanian University Students: Evidence from the Adult Eating Behaviour Questionnaire
item.description:
Dietetics
Background: The transition to university is a critical period during which young adults gain greater independence in eating and lifestyle behaviors. Appetitive traits may help characterize individual differences in eating behavior. Objective: This study aimed to examine associations between Adult Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (AEBQ) subscale scores and dietary-frequency, physical-activity, household-income, smoking, and BMI measures among Jordanian university students. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 485 students aged 18–24 years from three Jordanian universities (HU, UJ, and JUST). Face-to-face interviews collected sociodemographic, lifestyle, dietary, and AEBQ data, and anthropometric measurements were obtained to calculate BMI. Analyses included independent-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA with post hoc comparisons, Kendall’s tau-b correlations, Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction for dietary comparisons, and multivariable linear regression models. Results: Participants had a mean age of 21.34 ± 2.17 years; 37.9% reported smoking and 45.2% reported moderate physical activity. Mean AEBQ subscale scores were 2.85 ± 1.09 for Emotional Over-Eating, 3.84 ± 0.64 for Enjoyment of Food, 3.12 ± 0.83 for Hunger, 2.80 ± 0.74 for Food Fussiness, 2.94 ± 0.95 for Slowness in Eating, and 3.38 ± 0.83 for Satiety Responsiveness. In adjusted analyses, higher BMI was associated with higher Emotional Over-Eating and lower Satiety Responsiveness. Household income below 500 JOD (versus 500–1000 JOD) was associated with higher Hunger and Satiety Responsiveness, while income above 1000 JOD was associated with lower Slowness in Eating. Several dietary-frequency associations remained significant after FDR correction. Conclusion: AEBQ subscale scores were associated with selected characteristics in this sample. These cross-sectional associations do not establish causal relationships. The modified Arabic AEBQ and shortened food-frequency questionnaire require further evaluation in Jordanian populations.

item.title: Supplementation with cartilage hydrolysate and rosehip peel extract in physically active adults: main outcomes and exploratory findings of a randomized, placebo-controlled study on knee discomfort
item.description:
Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Background and objectives Joint discomfort and pain during physical activity are frequent conditions in healthy adults, which can lead to mobility limitations, with multiple consequences on health and quality of life. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a food supplement which combines cartilage hydrolysate and a rosehip extract on knee pain and discomfort in physically active healthy adults, examining subgroups according to sex and menopausal status. Methods In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 138 participants received either 4 capsules/day of Chondractiv™ Move (CM, containing 1200 mg/day of hydrolyzed chicken cartilage and 380 mg/day of Rosa canina extract) or a placebo (maltodextrin) for 8 weeks. Activity-related knee pain was assessed on a 0-10 eVAS following a standardized single-leg step-down test (SLSD) and analyzed via an ANCOVA. Activity-related knee pain experienced during or after daily activities (0-100 eVAS), daily life pain (ICOAP questionnaire), knee function (KOOS questionnaire), quality of life (SF-12 questionnaire) and range of motion were also assessed throughout the intervention period. Results Participants (39.9% men, 39.1% pre-menopausal women [PreMW] and 21.0% post-menopausal women [PostMW]) with a mean age of 46.4 years and a mean BMI of 24.4 kg/m 2 , practiced 5.6 hours of exercise per week on average. Knee pain after SLSD significantly decreased ( p < 0.0001) during the intervention in both arms in the entire population (CM: −2.2; placebo: −2.4), but with no significant difference between arms (delta −0.2 [95%CI −1.1; 0.7], p > 0.05). However, exploratory analyses in PostMW showed that the change from baseline tended to be greater with CM versus placebo (−3.4 versus −1.2; delta 2.2 [95%CI −0.2;4.7], p = 0.0712). Further exploration indicated a benefit of CM over placebo on knee pain experienced during daily activities (entire cohort; p = 0.0255) and after activity (PostMW only; p = 0.0421), and in the Sport and recreation dimension of the KOOS (PostMW; p = 0.0381). Quality of life and range of motion evolved favorably, but with no between-arm difference. Conclusions After eight weeks of supplementation, CM did not demonstrate superiority over placebo for the primary endpoint (pain after SLSD) but exploratory analyses indicated clinically meaningful improvements in postmenopausal women, particularly. These findings require confirmation in further large-scale studies. Clinical trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, identifier [NCT06714851].

item.title: Perioperative individualized nursing for an adolescent with recurrent tracheoesophageal fistula after endoscopic repair: a case report
item.description:
Frontiers in Pediatrics
Background Congenital esophageal atresia (CEA) type III is a common neonatal digestive malformation, and recurrent tracheoesophageal fistula (rTEF) is a refractory long-term postoperative complication. Combined suspension laryngoscopy and flexible bronchoscopy minimally invasive fistula repair is a novel therapeutic strategy, yet standardized perioperative nursing experience targeting adolescents with multiple failed transthoracic surgeries remains scarce. Conventional nursing cannot simultaneously manage compound risks including severe malnutrition, tracheomalacia, adolescent anxiety and airway edema. This case report aimed to summarize multidisciplinary team (MDT) individualized full-cycle nursing protocols for this rare patient population. Case presentation A 17.5-year-old male patient with rTEF, 17.5 years after neonatal primary congenital esophageal atresia repair, with two failed transthoracic fistula closures, presented persistent feeding choking, recurrent pneumonia and severe malnutrition (BMI=15.5 kg/m 2 ). MDT refined airway management, quantitative staged nutrition, whole-course psychological intervention and predictive complication prevention were implemented before and after endoscopic fistula repair. No severe complications occurred during hospitalization. Esophagography and bronchoscopy on postoperative day 10 confirmed complete fistula healing. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 14 with a 0.8 kg weight gain, and one-month follow-up showed sustained fistula repair and continuous weight improvement. Conclusion MDT-driven individualized perioperative nursing effectively reduces airway and nutritional complications and promotes fistula healing in adolescent rTEF patients receiving endoscopic minimally invasive surgery. This case provides replicable evidence-based nursing references for similar complex rare esophageal malformation cases.

item.title: Artificial intelligence-generated and algorithmically personalized music interventions and their effects on brain function, behavior, and health: a critical review
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener’s own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

item.title: Glycaemic screening before kidney transplantation should include an oral glucose tolerance test
item.description:
Frontiers in Nephrology
Presence of diabetes mellitus (diabetes) adversely affects outcomes after kidney transplantation, and glycaemic screening should be included in the pretransplant evaluation of kidney transplant recipients. However, there is limited evidence regarding the optimal glycaemic screening protocol and current practices vary. According to diagnostic criteria defined by the American Diabetes Association, diabetes may be diagnosed based on HbA1c or plasma glucose criteria, including either fasting plasma glucose or 2-hour plasma glucose during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 1 (OGTT). In asymptomatic patients who fulfil diagnostic criteria for diabetes, confirmatory testing is needed to establish the diagnosis 1 .KDIGO guidelines regard OGTT as the gold standard for pretransplant assessment of glycemia 2 . However, a European survey from the ERA DESCARTES Working Group indicates that this recommendation has not been universally implemented 3 . As part of the pretransplant work-up in Norway, all kidney transplant candidates without known diabetes routinely undergo assessment with both HbA1c and OGTT.This study aimed to determine the frequency and distribution of diabetes-range HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and 2-hour plasma glucose results among kidney transplant recipients without known diabetes. The assessments were made according to existing pretransplant protocol at the time the patients were evaluated for waitlisting.In this retrospective observational study, patients who received a kidney transplant in Norway between 2007 and 2022 (n=3290) were identified from the national transplant registry. We excluded patients with preexisting diabetes (n=724), patients listed for re-transplantation (n=26) or combined organ transplantation (n=22) as well as patients without available HbA1c or OGTT (n=466), leaving 2052 patients eligible for the study. Data describing HbA1c and OGTT were retrieved from the patients' electronic medical records. All patients have provided signed informed consent covering this kind of analyses and the study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics South-East (reference 407293). During the study period 2007-2022, 5.5% of patients died while waitlisted for kidney transplantation, 11.9% were permanently withdrawn from waiting list for kidney transplantation from various reasons. Among all patients waitlisted for kidney transplantation during the study period, 12 patients (0.4%) are still waiting for kidney transplantation. American Diabetes Association criteria for diabetes were used to define diabetes range glycaemic levels: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol or plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, or 2-hour plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L 1 .The proportion of patients fulfilling diabetes-range glycaemic levels were reported as rates or percentages and the distribution is illustrated in Figure 1 American Diabetes Association criteria for prediabetes were used to define prediabetes range glycaemic levels 1 : HbA1c from 39 to 47 mmol/mol or plasma glucose from 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L, or 2-hour plasma glucose from 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L.As part of the pretransplant work-up, HbA1c test and OGTT investigations were generally scheduled on a dialysis-free day, by the local nephrologist. OGTT test routines have been standardized in Norwegian hospitals throughout the study period. The OGTT was performed in the morning after at least 10 hours of fasting with oral administration of 75 grams of glucose in 200 mL of water when patients were seated and had avoided smoking the same day and were in their common medical state. They were instructed to stay on a weightmaintaining diet for 3 days prior to testing and abstain from alcohol. Plasma glucose was measured just prior to, 30 and 120 min after the glucose load and HbA1c was also assessed in a pre-OGTT sample. HbA1c analyses have been standardized in Norwegian hospitals since 2007 with standardized high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) or immunochemical methods certified by the IFCC in accredited laboratories. HbA1c and OGTT test results were sent to the national transplant centre as part of transplant candidate evaluation. The year of glycaemic testing, but not the exact date, was available for this study.In case of repeated tests, only the closest OGTT preformed prior to being waitlisted for transplantation were available in this analysis.This study included results from 2052 kidney transplant recipients (1354 males /66%) with mean age at transplantation 54 years (range:18-83 years) and mean BMI was 25.8 kg/m 2 (range:16.0-36.2 kg/m 2 ). Thirty percent of the patients were transplanted pre-emptively, while 47% were in haemodialysis and 23% in peritoneal dialysis before transplantation. The mean time from the OGTT/HbA1c assessment to transplantation was 1.62 years (range 0-8).We identified 165 kidney transplant recipients (8%) without known diabetes with glycaemic test results within the diabetes range detected during pretransplant work-up. Out of these, 48 patients fulfilled the HbA1c criterion, 23 patients the fasting plasma glucose criterion while 122 fulfilled the 2-hour plasma glucose criterion (Figure 1). In 23 cases, more than one diagnostic criterion was met. Baseline BMI was comparable between included and excluded patients, but excluded patients were on average five years younger than those included.Additional data are available in supplementary material.If 2-hr glucose tests results were excluded, only 65 patients (39%) were found to have glycaemic test results within the diabetes range. This approach with HbA1c and/or fasting plasma glucose assessment only, revealed 39% of the cases compared to when 2-hour plasma glucose data were included in the analyses.Among the remaining 1887 patients without diabetes-range glycaemic test results, 976 patients (52%) had test results within range of prediabetes according to one or several ADA criteria (HbA1c criterion n=514, fasting glucose criterion n= 417, 2-hour plasma glucose criterion n= 449).The main finding of our study was that 8% of Norwegian kidney transplant recipients without known diabetes were identified at the time for waitlisting with pretransplant diabetes-range glycaemic levels. These findings are in accordance with the results from two smaller studies from Austria (n=138) and Spain (n=186) which detected 3% and 6% respectively with diabetes-range screening results among their patients waitlisted for kidney transplantation [4][5] .In our study, the vast majority (74%) were identified through the 2-hour plasma glucose criterion. These patients would likely have been missed for further diagnostics and follow-up if the pre-waitlisting OGTT screening had not been included. While some transplant centres prefer fasting glucose and HbA1c and not OGTT in this clinical setting, our findings support the inclusion of OGTT as the gold standard for pretransplant glucose assessment as recommended in KDIGO guidelines 2 . Discrepancies between HbA1c and OGTT test results have also been described in the general population 6 and among kidney transplanted patients 7 . Additionally, it is known that HbA1c has its limitations to correctly reflect glycaemia in patients with chronic kidney disease 8 . In the present study, we lack information on whether the pre-waitlisting test findings triggered a follow-up re-test and/or treatment of diabetes or preventive efforts in prediabetes, and we suggest that such measures should be implemented. Hyperglycaemia identified before transplantation can be used to discuss a tailored approach to lifestyle or pharmacological interventions, when appropriate. In cases of overweight/obesity, weight loss can prevent diabetes to develop but also put diabetes into remission when identified early 9 . Since both prediabetes and diabetes are associated with increased mortality and cardiovascular risk after kidney transplantation [10][11] , pretransplant OGTT test results can be utilized in a continuous risk assessment for post-transplant diabetes among other post-transplant outcomes, as recommended by the 2022 PTDM Consensus Meeting 12 . Some transplant centres consider use of a less diabetogenic immunosuppressive regimen for patients at increased risk after kidney transplantation 13 .A strength of our study is the relative large national cohort of Norwegian kidney transplant recipients without known diabetes, with available HbA1c and OGTT sampled as part of systemic and standardized pretransplant work up, which allowed this study to analyse the overlap among individual screening thresholds. Our study has some limitations. Treatment data on anaemia, blood-transfusions, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and iron supplementation were unfortunately not available for this study. Reported measurements of HbA1c and OGTT were performed only once per patient, while confirmative measurement is advocated in asymptomatic subjects before establishing a diabetes diagnosis 1 . OGTT is well known to have limited reproducibility and our study cohort included primarily data from patients who were transplanted and were predominantly Caucasian, limiting generalizability to all transplant candidates and other ethnic groups.In this cohort of kidney transplant recipients without previously known diabetes who underwent pretransplant glycaemic assessment, 8% had at least one screening result within the diabetes range. Notably, most cases were identified through the 2-hour plasma glucose criterion. These findings suggest that reliance on HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose alone may miss patients who warrant further diagnostics and follow-up for diabetes.

item.title: Autonomous digital lifestyle intervention for obesity: a comparative study of software-generated vs. provider-delivered body composition outcomes
item.description:
Frontiers in Digital Health
Background Many lifestyle intervention apps for weight management rely on human coaching, which increases cost and variability, or use calorie-counting approaches that lack structured, individualized guidance. Fully autonomous digital platforms that deliver personalized nutrition and exercise plans with body composition tracking remain limited. Objective To compare an autonomous, protein-focused digital lifestyle intervention (RightBMI App) with provider-delivered lifestyle intervention for weight loss and body composition outcomes in metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) candidates. Materials and methods This prospective quasi-experimental study enrolled 160 patients at a single center (April 2024–April 2025). Patients were sequentially allocated to the RightBMI App ( n = 80) or provider-delivered care ( n = 80). Outcomes (% total body weight loss [%TBWL], % fat mass loss [%FML], % visceral fat loss [%VFL], and % muscle mass loss [%MML]) were assessed over 24 weeks using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) with multiple imputation and inverse probability weighting, adjusting for age, Body Mass Index (BMI), and sex. A time-to-event analysis (Kaplan–Meier and Cox proportional hazards) was performed as the primary sensitivity analysis to address informative censoring due to MBS clearance at ≥10% TBWL. Results In GEE models, the App group showed significantly greater %TBWL at weeks 12 (+2.64%, p < 0.001) and 16 (+2.47%, p = 0.027), and greater %FML at weeks 12 (+2.94%, p = 0.028) and 16 (+4.20%, p = 0.003) compared with provider-delivered care. By week 24, outcomes were comparable (%TBWL: 20.01% vs. 19.97%; %FML: 36.81% vs. 35.74%). Both groups achieved substantial fat mass loss while preserving muscle mass. Time-to-event analysis showed no significant difference in time to ≥10% TBWL (log-rank p = 0.23; adjusted HR 0.83, p = 0.43). The App group had a higher MBS clearance rate by week 24 (90% vs. 71.25%, p = 0.0023) with low attrition. User satisfaction was high (mean 8.76/10). Conclusion The autonomous RightBMI App demonstrated greater mid-study weight and fat loss compared with provider-delivered care after statistical adjustment, with comparable 24-week outcomes and effective muscle preservation. Time-to-event analysis showed no significant difference in time to achieve ≥10% TBWL. These findings support the potential of fully autonomous digital platforms as scalable alternatives to traditional provider-led interventions in MBS candidates. Limitations include the non-randomized design and use of consumer-grade bioimpedance scales.

item.title: Subjective and mobile EEG responses to wood-clad and drywall interior environments: An in situ crossover study
item.description:
[预印本] 来源未提供
Exposure to natural environments has been associated with benefits for health and wellbeing, and natural materials offer one avenue for introducing nature-associated elements into interiors. However, relatively little in situ research has examined subjective and neural responses to full-scale interiors with contrasting material characteristics. In this within-subject crossover study, 36 students completed 10-min immersions in wood-clad and white drywall prototype pods following a mental arithmetic task while self-report data and mobile electroencephalography (EEG) were collected. Adjusted models indicated greater momentary nature connectedness and perceived restorative qualities in the wood-clad pod, as well as higher hedonic tone and energetic arousal and lower stress. The primary frontal EEG measures did not differ significantly between pods after correction for multiple comparisons. Together, these findings show that contrasting full-scale interiors elicited distinct immediate subjective responses without corresponding robust differences in selected frontal EEG measures, highlighting the value of multimodal in situ approaches for studying architectural experience.

item.title: Síndrome de rumiación en un niño con encefalopatía crónica severa
item.description:
Archivos de Pediatría del Uruguay
Introduction: rumination syndrome (RS) is an uncommon functional gastrointestinal disorder. It is characterized by repeated regurgitation of recently ingested food, which does not occur during sleep and is not preceded by nausea. It occurs in the absence of an underlying organic disease to account for the symptoms.Objectives: to describe the diagnostic and therapeutic management of RS in a child with severe chronic encephalopathy.Case presentation: an 8-year-old male with severe static (non-progressive) chronic encephalopathy and clinical dysphagia. He demonstrated normal growth until age 6. One year prior to the consultation, he developed frequent postprandial regurgitations without retching or nausea, accompanied by rumination. Symptoms resolved during sleep. Physical examination revealed an emaciated appearance, reduced muscle mass, and depleted subcutaneous fat. Body mass index (BMI) was 11,5 < P5 (z-score = -4.0). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) demonstrated grade III gastroesophageal reflux. Daytime oral feeding was fractionated, and complete formula was administered via continuous nocturnal gastroclysis; omeprazole was initiated, and a therapeutic trial of baclofen was conducted. The patient showed favorable progress and was discharged after 25 days with gained weight, receiving oral nutrition.Discussion: RS is a poorly recognized entity. Its diagnosis is primarily clinical and one of exclusion. High-resolution esophageal manometry combined with impedance testing is the gold standard when the clinical presentation is ambiguous. An interdisciplinary and multimodal therapeutic approach is required. Cognitive-behavioral therapy cannot be used in children with severe neurological impairment. Treatment with baclofen represents a viable therapeutic option. Careful follow-up planning is essential to monitor treatment response and potential adverse effects.

item.title: ATTENTION AGGREGATION U-NET++ (AAUNET++) AND DIFFUSION BASED VARIATIONAL AUTOENCODER (DVAE) FOR EPILEPTIC SEIZURE DETECTION
item.description:
International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
To monitor brain electrical activity and identify unusual spikes or asymmetries that can point to a seizure, electroencephalograms (EEG), are mostly utilised in epileptic seizure detection.However, it takes a lot of time for experts to visually examine an EEG, and their diagnoses could even conflict.For EEG diagnoses, an automated computer-aided diagnosis is therefore required.The Multivariate Variational Mode Decomposition (MVMD) algorithm for EEG signal denoising is suggested in this study.Construction of multivariate oscillations is based on the assumption that the same frequency element must be present in all channels of the input EEG data.Recovery of signals that have inherent multivariate modulated oscillations from multivariate input EEG data, a variational optimisation problem is developed for signal denoising.Attention Aggregation U-Net++ (AAUNET++) model has been developed for feature extraction.The original multi-level skip connections of U-net++ are replaced in the feature extraction process by attention aggregation, which is introduced to capture global contextual information.Diffusion Based Variational Autoencoder (DVAE) is introduced for seizure detection in EEG signals.DVAE integrates the probabilistic latent representation capability of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with the progressive noise modeling of a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) to achieve robust feature learning and enhanced noise suppression in EEG.Using the Children's Hospital Boston-Massachusetts Institute of Technology (CHB-MIT) scalp EEG database, the recommended method attains superior efficiency by precision (PRE), recall/sensitivity, F-measure (F-score), and accuracy (ACC).

item.title: A Nomogram Model for Rheumatoid Arthritis-Related Low Muscle Strength was Developed Based on the HALP Score Combined With Clinical Characteristics
item.description:
Discovery Medicine
Background: Low muscle strength is a common but underrecognized complication of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), associated with functional disability, impaired mobility, reduced quality of life, and adverse health outcomes. This study aimed to identify factors associated with low muscle strength in RA patients and evaluate the incremental value of the hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocyte, and platelet (HALP) score for its identification.Methods: This retrospective multicenter study included patients with RA who were hospitalized in the Departments of Nephrology, Rheumatology and Immunology at Jinhua Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine and Lanxi Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine between January 2022 and June 2026. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with low muscle strength. Multicollinearity among candidate variables was assessed using the variance inflation factor (VIF). To evaluate the incremental value of HALP beyond the clinical-variable selection process, the Clinical Base Model was initially established without including HALP. After the Clinical Base Model was finalized, HALP was added as a single additional variable to construct the nested Base + HALP Model. The incremental discriminative performance of the HALP score was evaluated by comparing changes in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ΔAUC), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and net reclassification improvement (NRI). Decision curve analysis (DCA) was performed to assess the estimated net benefit of each model across a range of risk thresholds. Internal validation was conducted using bootstrap resampling, and sensitivity analysis was performed among patients aged ≥50 years using the same analytical procedures.Results: A total of 220 patients with RA were included, of whom 81 (36.8%) had low muscle strength. Compared with patients without low muscle strength, those with low muscle strength were older, had lower body mass index (BMI) and HALP scores, higher erythrocyte sedimentation rate disease activity score (DAS28-ESR) values, and were more likely to be female. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified age, sex, BMI, DAS28-ESR, current glucocorticoid (GC) use, and HALP score as independent factors associated with low muscle strength. The clinical base model demonstrated an apparent AUC of 0.784 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.722–0.847). After the addition of the HALP score, the AUC increased to 0.829 (95% CI, 0.775–0.883), with a ΔAUC of 0.045 (DeLong test, p = 0.020). The Base + HALP model also demonstrated improved classification performance, with an NRI of 0.663 (95% CI, 0.402–0.924; p = 0.001) and an IDI of 0.072 (95% CI, 0.039–0.107; p = 0.002). After 1000-bootstrap internal validation, the AUCs of the clinical base and Base + HALP model were 0.766 (95% CI, 0.707–0.826) and 0.809 (95% CI, 0.757–0.863), respectively. Decision curve analysis demonstrated that the Base + HALP model provided a greater estimated net benefit than the clinical base model and the treat-all and treat-none strategies, particularly across threshold probabilities from approximately 10% to 60%.Conclusions: The HALP score, age, sex, BMI, DAS28-ESR and current GC use were independently associated with low muscle strength in patients with RA. The Base + HALP Model demonstrated good discrimination, calibration and estimated net benefit. However, further independent external validation and prospective studies are still needed in the future to clarify the role of this model.

item.title: Proton Signaling Biology From Ancient Bioenergetics to Neural Communication: An Exploration of Keratan Sulfate as a Potential Proton-Modulatory Molecule
item.description:
Discovery Medicine
This mini review examines the potential roles of proton signaling in the peripheral and central nervous systems and its proposed regulation by keratan sulfate (KS). Protons are central to bioenergetics and rapid chemical signaling, linking metabolism to membrane excitability and receptor activity across tissues. Nanoscale-to-microscale pH transients may add a further layer of intercellular communication in the nervous system through proton-sensitive ion channels and receptors. Extracellular matrix glycosaminoglycans may influence this signaling by buffering and transporting protons. Keratan sulfate has an unusually high capacity to bind and conduct protons. Evidence from electrolocation biology, proton-conductive biomaterials, and brain proton sensors suggests that keratan sulfate may act as a local proton reservoir and shuttle within defined microenvironments, thereby shaping pH-dependent neuromodulatory processes in health and disease. KS-substituted proteoglycans have the potential to act as neuron modulatory molecules mediating effects on cellular metabolism. KS shows considerable promise as a neuromodulatory molecule. Further electrophysiological studies are warranted using KS knockout animal models to test this hypothesis and validate the proposed role of KS as a potential regulatory neural interface molecule.

item.title: Challenges of war: paroxysmal disorders in military personnel. Observational experience and optimization of differential diagnosis
item.description:
EMERGENCY MEDICINE
Background. An unprecedented increase in paroxysmal events among military personnel is observed in the context of intensive combat operations. Up to 40–50 % of cases initially diagnosed as seizure disorders are, in fact, psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES), or functional seizures. This study purposed to analyze the underlying neurobiological mechanisms, optimize differential diagnostic algorithms, and personalize the treatment of epileptic and conversion seizures within this patient cohort. Materials and methods. A narrative literature review was conducted to evaluate current neurobiological concepts regarding the development of post-traumatic epilepsy and PNES in military personnel with blast-induced trauma, post-concussion syndrome, and post-traumatic stress disorder, supplemented by a retrospective analysis of proprietary clinic observational experience with military personnel at the Kharkiv Military Medical Clinical Center of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine. Results. The pathogenesis of PNES is conceptualized via the “dual-hit” hypothesis: organic diffuse axonal injury disrupts the top-down inhibitory control of the prefrontal cortex over the stress-hyperactivated amygdala, likely resulting in the somatic conversion of affect. An adaptive, step-wise diagnostic algorithm for forward medical evacuation stages was established. In the absence of electroencephalography, the primary diagnostic tools are the bedside clinical evaluation of ictal semiology and video recording of the events using available mobile devices. Differentiated therapeutic strategies are substantiated. For post-traumatic epilepsy, novel anti-seizure medications are the drugs of choice, carefully weighing the risk of neuropsychiatric adverse effects associated with levetiracetam against the mood-stabilizing benefits of lamotrigine. For PNES, prescribing antiseizure medications constitutes an iatrogenic error; the foundational management strategy relies on deprescribing, the administration of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and cognitive-behavioral therapy. Conclusions. Shifting the nosological paradigm (overcoming the stereotype that all seizures equate to epilepsy) and adopting a multidisciplinary neuropsychiatric approach are critical. This is essential to avoid neurotoxic polypharmacy, prevent unjustified medical discharge, and maintain the operational readiness of military personnel.

item.title: Image quality and radiation dose optimization in CT pulmonary angiography using 120, 100, and 80 kV protocols for pulmonary thromboembolism diagnosis
item.description:
Quantitative Imaging in Medicine and Surgery
Background: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the standard imaging modality for diagnosing pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE). Lowering tube potential enhances iodine attenuation but may affect image noise. This retrospective study evaluated quantitative image quality, subjective ratings, and radiation dose across 120, 100, and 80 kV CTPA protocols on a dual-source CT scanner. Methods: Ninety adult patients (n=30 per protocol) undergoing clinically indicated CTPA were evaluated across three tube potential settings (120, 100, and 80 kV). Quantitative parameters pulmonary artery attenuation [Hounsfield unit (HU)], image noise [standard deviation (SD)], signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and size-specific dose estimates (SSDE)—were evaluated. Three cardiothoracic radiologists performed blinded qualitative assessments using a 5-point Likert scale. Radiation dose metrics [volumetric computed tomography dose index (CTDIvol), dose-length product (DLP), and estimated effective dose] were recorded. Results: Baseline characteristics [age, sex, body mass index (BMI)] were comparable across groups (P>0.05). Pulmonary artery attenuation increased significantly as tube potential decreased, reaching highest values at 80 kV (633.9±92.1 vs. 338.5±42.1 HU at 120 kV, P<0.001). Image noise increased modestly at 80 kV (25.88±5.0 vs. 20.23±4.1 HU, P=0.26). SNR and CNR were significantly higher at 80 kV (25.93±2.6 and 25.20±3.4) compared with 120 kV (18.19±4.8 and 9.31±2.1, P<0.001). Effective dose decreased significantly by 46.4% from 3.34±0.67 mSv (120 kV) to 1.79±0.35 mSv (80 kV) (P<0.001). Qualitative scores for overall image quality, vascular enhancement, and motion artifacts showed no significant differences across protocols (P>0.05). Conclusions: Lowering tube potential to 80 kV in CTPA significantly increases vascular attenuation, SNR, and CNR while offering substantial radiation dose savings and maintaining subjective image quality scores. These findings support the feasibility of an 80-kV protocol for radiation dose optimization in CTPA.

item.title: Decoding motor imagery EEG signals by a deep learning network integrating multiscale filtering and temporal-channel attention mechanisms
item.description:
PLoS ONE
Due to their low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationarity, accurately classifying EEG signals is still one of the main hindrances that limit the real-world applications of a brain-computer interface (BCI). Deep learning (DL) is a potential method for addressing the problem. However, how to create a suitable DL network for motor imagery (MI)-based BCIs poses severe challenges in the case of insufficient training data. In this paper, a DL network based on multiscale convolutional neural network (CNN) and temporal and channel attention mechanisms is proposed for decoding MI tasks. Temporal and spatial features are extracted by four parallel CNN branches, each of which is followed by a Transformer block for learning the global correlations of local time features. The outputs from the four Transformer blocks are concatenated along channel dimension and then input into a channel attention module for channel fusion. The subsequent feature map is classified by a CNN, which replaces the commonly used fully connected layer for reducing computational complexity. The proposed network was evaluated on three publicly available BCI datasets and compared with five state-of-the-art DL networks. The training data sets are augmented using the approach segmentation and reconstruction. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed network achieved an average accuracy of 80.21% on Dataset 1 (4-class tasks), 90.19% on Dataset 2 (2-class tasks), and 97.32% on Dataset 3 (4-class tasks), surpassing the strongest baselines FBCNet on Dataset 1, MSFBCNN on Dataset 2 and MSFBCNN on Dataset 3 by 2.59%, 1.27%, and 1.99% respectively. The network effectively decoded the MI-based EEG signals, providing a potential method for BCI applications.

item.title: Investigating the relationship between polycystic ovary syndrome, personality type, and adherence to the Mediterranean dietary pattern in infertile women: a case-control study
item.description:
BMC Nutrition
Reproduction is fundamental to population growth and the social and economic well-being of societies. Hormonal disorders, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), which result from hormonal imbalances, may disrupt ovulation and lead to infertility. Various factors, including genetics, mental health, insulin resistance, and nutrition, contribute to the development of this syndrome. This study aimed to investigate the associations among polycystic ovary syndrome, personality type, and adherence to the Mediterranean dietary pattern in infertile women. In this descriptive analytical case-control study, 180 non-pregnant women aged 18 to 45 years with a history of infertility were evaluated, including 90 women with PCOS and 90 infertile women without PCOS. Demographic information was collected using a general characteristics questionnaire. Dietary intake was assessed using a validated Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ), and adherence to the Mediterranean diet was quantified by calculating a Mediterranean Diet Score derived from FFQ data, while personality type was evaluated using the NEO-FFI questionnaire. The relationship between PCOS, personality type, and adherence to the Mediterranean dietary pattern was analyzed using SPSS version 23, with a significance level set at 0.05. Regarding personality type, no statistically significant differences were observed between the case and control groups in the variables of conscientiousness ( p = 0.87), Eagerness for new experiences ( p = 0.26), extraversion/introversion ( p = 0.14), agreeableness ( p = 0.44), and neuroticism ( p = 0.81). Similarly, there was no statistically significant difference between the groups in terms of personality type or Mediterranean diet adherence scores. Furthermore, no statistically significant relationship was found between adherence to the Mediterranean dietary pattern and the presence of PCOS ( p = 0.87). The findings of this study did not demonstrate statistically significant associations among polycystic ovary syndrome, personality traits, and adherence to the Mediterranean dietary pattern among the infertile women. However, because BMI, physical activity, insulin resistance, and other major metabolic and lifestyle variables were not assessed, the absence of an observed association between Mediterranean diet adherence and PCOS should be interpreted with caution and should not be regarded as evidence of an association independent of these potential confounders. Future investigations employing longitudinal designs, mediation analysis, or structural equation modeling are warranted to better elucidate these complex interrelationships.

item.title: The effect of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) Training on emotion regulation during voluntary inpatient care for youth with mixed mental health conditions
item.description:
Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health
Adolescence is a sensitive period for emotional and cognitive development, with heightened risk for mental health challenges, particularly in individuals with ADHD and affective disorders. While Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) improves emotion regulation and cognition in healthy populations, its effects in clinically complex adolescents are less understood. This pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) examined the exploratory impact of an 8-week MBSR program on behavioral performance and neural processing in 31 adolescents (12–18 years) enrolled in a live-in mental health program, with 14 assigned to MBSR and 17 to a non-MBSR group receiving standard care. Participants completed a modified emotional oddball task while behavioral responses and event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded. Results suggested that routine care with integrated MBSR was associated with selectively enhanced performance for fearful stimuli. Participants in the MBSR group showed shorter baseline-adjusted reaction times to fear-related stimuli and to targets following other targets, possibly reflecting improved task-relevant processing. ERP analyses detected no significant Group × Condition interactions for the P100 or P300 components, providing no evidence of broad changes in early sensory or attentional processing. In contrast, the MBSR group showed smaller baseline-adjusted Late Positive Potential (LPP) amplitudes for fearful stimuli but larger amplitudes for targets following fearful or other target stimuli, possibly reflecting attenuated sustained neural reactivity to threat and selective engagement with behaviorally relevant events. These patterns suggest that integrating MBSR into routine care may be associated with improved behavioral performance and selective modulation of later neural processing, potentially supporting rapid attentional engagement and efficient allocation of cognitive resources in adolescents with ADHD and affective disorders. This study suggests that mindfulness may have potential for supporting emotion regulation and attentional efficiency in clinical youth, while highlighting the need for larger-scale trials and examination of the long-term durability of these effects. Registered Clinical Trial (RCT) This study is part of a registered clinical trial. The trial protocol was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov under the registration identifier: NCT01307943.

item.title: Association between physical fitness and core emergency competencies among emergency nurses in China
item.description:
BMC Nursing
Emergency nurses require exceptional levels of clinical professionalism and physical fitness. However, little is known about the association between physical fitness and core emergency competencies among emergency nurses. The aims of this study were to describe the levels of physical fitness among emergency nurses and to explore the influence of physical fitness on their core emergency competencies. A descriptive and cross-sectional study among emergency nurses was conducted in China between April and May 2024. Data were collected using physical fitness tests and a self-reported questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, core emergency competencies, self-perceived health-reported physical fitness(HRPF), and the perceived associations between HRPF and core emergency competencies, mental fitness and attention. Multiple linear regression analysis was used to explore the association between physical fitness indicators and core emergency competencies. A total of 146 emergency nurses were enrolled. Of them, 3.4% had good physical fitness, 47.3% had general physical fitness, and 49.3% had poor physical fitness. Furthermore, 88.4% agreed that their HRPF was associated with their core emergency competencies. Multivariate analysis indicated that core emergency competencies were associated with self-reported HRPF (β’=0.288, 95%CI:3.001 ~ 10.746, P = 0.001) and choice reaction time (β’=-0.213, 95%CI:-75.805~-6.868, P = 0.019). After adjusting for sex, age and work tenure, self-reported HRPF (β’=0.254, 95%CI: 2.440 ~ 9.666, P = 0.001) and choice reaction time (β’=-0.217, 95%CI: -74.239~-10.064, P = 0.010) remained significant, and body mass index(BMI) was also positively associated with core emergency competencies (β’=0.261, 95%CI: 0.120 ~ 0.989, P = 0.013). Nearly half of the emergency nurses had poor physical fitness. Self-reported HRPF, BMI, and choice reaction time were all found to be related to the core emergency competencies. Nurse managers should prioritize developing programs to improve emergency nurses’ physical fitness factors associated with their core emergency competencies.

item.title: Comparison of functional recovery and complications between varus and valgus knees after total knee arthroplasty: a large-sample cohort study
item.description:
BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders
Abstract Objective To compare functional recovery, pain patterns, analgesic requirements, and postoperative complications between patients with varus and valgus deformities who underwent primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA), and to evaluate the clinical impact of lower limb alignment on prognosis. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 1,547 patients who underwent primary TKA for knee osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis at the Department of Joint Orthopedics, People’s Hospital of Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, between January 2020 and December 2023. Patients were divided according to the preoperative hip-knee-ankle (HKA) angle into the varus group (HKA < -3°, n = 1,356) and the valgus group (HKA > 3°, n = 191). Baseline characteristics, surgical data, and follow-up outcomes were collected, including Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) knee score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), and Forgotten Joint Score (FJS-12). Complications, revision rates, patient satisfaction, and analgesic use were also recorded. Results No significant differences were observed between the two groups in age, follow-up duration, BMI, WOMAC, or FJS-12 scores ( P > 0.05, d < 0.2). The valgus group had significantly higher ASA scores (2.30 vs. 2.17, P < 0.001, d = 0.33) and longer symptom duration (9.52 vs. 8.12 years, P < 0.001, d = 0.49), but significantly lower postoperative HSS scores (75.96 vs. 84.20, P < 0.001, d = 0.78). Univariable analysis revealed that the valgus group had higher rates of dissatisfaction (16.8% vs. 7.5%, P < 0.001, φ = 0.108) and persistent pain (34.0% vs. 18.9%, P < 0.001, φ = 0.123), whereas revision rates did not differ significantly (1.57% vs. 0.59%, P = 0.131, φ = 0.038). Stratified analysis revealed a significant interaction between deformity type and disease type (Breslow-Day P < 0.001). In OA patients, valgus deformity was associated with a markedly higher risk of dissatisfaction (OR = 11.05, 95% CI 5.92–20.58, P < 0.001). In RA patients, no significant difference was observed (OR = 0.63, 95% CI 0.23–1.69, P = 0.350). Daily analgesic use was significantly more frequent in the valgus group (38.5% vs. 15.6%, OR = 3.38, P < 0.001, φ = 0.228). Conclusion The effect of valgus deformity on postoperative satisfaction depends on disease type. In OA patients, valgus deformity significantly increases the risk of dissatisfaction; in RA patients, no significant difference is observed between valgus and varus groups. RA itself was associated with a higher overall dissatisfaction rate.Valgus deformity is also associated with a distinctive walking-pain phenotype and higher analgesic dependence, but revision rates were not significantly different. Clinical decision-making should stratify by disease type rather than relying on coronal alignment alone.

item.title: Evaluation of echocardiographic abnormalities and associated factors in 100 hemodialysis patients
item.description:
BMC Medical Imaging
Abstract Background Systematic assessment of cardiac remodeling in hemodialysis (HD) patients is essential for cardiovascular risk stratification. Echocardiography is a widely available tool for evaluating structural and functional cardiac abnormalities. We investigated associations between clinical and dialysis-related parameters and echocardiographic abnormalities among patients receiving chronic HD at the Dezful Nephrology Center in southwestern Iran. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 160 adults undergoing chronic HD were screened and 100 met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. All participants underwent transthoracic echocardiography. Associations between echocardiographic abnormalities and age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, body mass index (BMI), dyslipidemia, coronary and non-coronary vascular disease, dialysis access type, dialysis vintage, anemia, plasma lipid concentrations, and resting heart rate were evaluated Bivariate analyses were followed by multivariable logistic regression for prespecified binary echocardiographic outcomes. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. A two-sided P -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Echocardiographic abnormalities were present in 86% of patients. After multivariable adjustment, hypertension (aOR 2.80, 95% CI 1.30–6.00), coronary artery disease (aOR 6.10, 95% CI 1.90–19.60), non-coronary vascular disease (aOR 4.20, 95% CI 1.30–13.60), and lower plasma triglycerides (aOR 0.99 per mg/dL, 95% CI 0.98–0.995) were independently associated with left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Diabetes was associated with diastolic dysfunction (aOR 2.60, 95% CI 1.10–6.20) and moderate-to-severe mitral or tricuspid regurgitation (aOR 2.40, 95% CI 1.00–5.70). Dialysis access type and non-coronary vascular disease were linked to left ventricular hypertrophy. Lower plasma triglycerides, higher resting heart rate, and non-coronary vascular disease were associated with right ventricular abnormality. Lower BMI and lower plasma triglycerides were associated with a higher aortic index. Traditional risk factors together with dialysis-related parameters, particularly low serum triglycerides, low BMI, and arteriovenous fistula access, showed independent associations with specific echocardiographic phenotypes. Conclusion Echocardiographic abnormalities are highly prevalent in this HD cohort and independently associated with both traditional cardiovascular risk factors and selected dialysis-related parameters, including low plasma triglycerides, low BMI, and the presence of arteriovenous fistula. These findings support closer clinical attention to these variables for cardiac risk stratification in hemodialysis patients. Given the cross-sectional design and modest sample size, the results represent associations rather than causal effects. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

item.title: Biophysically constrained learning from healthy neural priors improves motor decoding in pathological cortical networks
item.description:
Science Advances
High-performance brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) rely on stable neural representations, yet brain functional impairments inherently disrupt canonical encoding, creating a fundamental decoding paradox. Conventional data-driven approaches struggle to bridge this gap because of pathological data scarcity and heterogeneity. Here, we propose to leverage healthy neural priors and introduce Pathology-Aware Consensus Training (PACT), a paradigm embedding biophysical constraints into healthy neural recordings to guide neural decoding. In a gesture classification task using high-density electrocorticography from patients with gliomas infiltrating the motor cortex, PACT improved the accuracy by more than 10%, effectively restoring the distorted semantic geometry of motor commands and realigning them with healthy canonical representations (correlation increase: r = 0.66 to r = 0.94). Mechanistically, PACT induced an emergent “inverse weighting” strategy: The model autonomously suppresses high-power pathological noise while reanchoring spatial attention to functional compensatory regions. This study provides a proof of concept for improving decoding in compromised networks by harnessing healthy neural dynamics, laying the theoretical foundation for future BCI deployments in clinical populations.

item.title: The Influence of Facial Attractiveness on Empathy: A Systematic Review
item.description:
Japanese Psychological Research
Abstract This systematic review examines the impact of facial attractiveness on empathic responses. By synthesizing findings from behavioral studies, EEG, fMRI, EMG, and fNIRS research, it examines whether and how attractiveness modulates empathy at cognitive and emotional levels. The results indicate that attractive faces often trigger stronger automatic empathic reactions, likely driven by emotional contagion and positive beauty stereotypes. Conversely, in conscious empathic tasks or those requiring cognitive effort, greater empathy tends to be shown towards less attractive individuals. Significant differences related to gender, moral context, and participant experience reveal the relationship between physical attractiveness and empathy. Overall, facial attractiveness has a significant impact on empathy; however, its influence varies depending on the type of empathic process and the experimental conditions. This review offers new insights into distinguishing the affective and cognitive components of empathy and suggests ways to manipulate empathic responses through physical appearance cues.

item.title: A bibliometric analysis of combat stress during 1990–2024 from Web of Science database
item.description:
Journal of Workplace Behavioral Health
The aims of this study were to explore the research hotspots and trends in combat stress worldwide. Using the Web of Science (WoS) as the literature source, we searched for papers published between 1990 and 2024 using combat stress-related terms combined with veteran-related terms. VOSviewer 1.6.17 and CiteSpace 6.2R6 software were employed to analyze the data. A bibliometric analysis was applied to assess the publications related to combat stress. In total, 5840 publications were retrieved. Analysis of the keywords indicated that memory, moral injury, military personnel, prazosin, secondary traumatization, traumatic brain injury, cardiovascular disease, high-density EEG, traumatic stress disorder, and milieu therapy were the main research hotspots in the field of combat stress. The burst detection indicated that the psychological coping mechanism of combat stress, particularly resilience, is a future research trend. These results can provide insight into the research progress regarding combat stress.

item.title: Generalizable neural decoding for clinically scalable brain-computer interfaces
item.description:
npj Biomedical Innovations.
Brain–computer interfaces promise restored communication and movement, yet accuracy achieved under development rarely survives new sessions, users, tasks, or hardware. Generalization, not peak performance, determines clinical scalability. Here we examine generalizable neural decoding from development to deployment, organized by the domain held out at evaluation, target-data access, adaptation strategy, and the clinical conditions under which performance persists, identifying benchmarking standards, prospective validation, and hardware-algorithm co-design as prerequisites for durable benefit.

item.title: Lighting design for enclosed environments: A multimodal predictive framework for human alertness and emotional responses
item.description:
Advanced Design Research
